name: Egypt
modern: Egypt (the Nile Valley, Delta, and Sinai)
era: c. 3100 BC – 30 BC; central to Genesis and Exodus (c. 2000–1200 BC) and again under the divided monarchy
religion: Polytheistic. Egyptians worshiped Ra, Amun, Osiris, Isis, Horus, Ptah and many others, and regarded Pharaoh himself as divine. Burial rites and temple cults were central to life. The plagues of Exodus confront these gods (Exodus 12:12).
leaders: Pharaoh of Joseph’s day (unnamed; Genesis 41)
Pharaoh of the Exodus (unnamed; Exodus 1–14)
Shishak / Shoshenq I, who raided Jerusalem (1 Kings 14:25)
Necho II, who killed Josiah at Megiddo (2 Kings 23:29)
Hophra / Apries (Jeremiah 44:30)
story: Abram sheltered here during famine, Joseph rose to govern it, and Israel was enslaved here until Moses led the exodus. Later kings alternately allied with Egypt and were warned against trusting it. Mary and Joseph fled here with the infant Jesus (Matthew 2).

name: Cush (Nubia)
modern: Southern Egypt, Sudan, and northern Ethiopia/Eritrea
religion: Polytheistic. Nubians worshiped Amun (with a major temple at Jebel Barkal), along with Apedemak, the lion god, and other Egyptian-influenced deities.
leaders: Zerah the Cushite, defeated by Asa (2 Chronicles 14)
Tirhakah (Taharqa), king of Cush who marched against Assyria (2 Kings 19:9)
Ebed-melech the Cushite, who rescued Jeremiah (Jeremiah 38)
The Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, whose treasurer met Philip (Acts 8:27)
story: Moses married a Cushite woman (Numbers 12). Cush appears as a distant, powerful land in the prophets, and in Acts the gospel reaches an Ethiopian official.

name: Israel & Canaan
modern: Israel and the Palestinian territories (with southern Lebanon and the Golan at the northern edge)
religion: Canaanites practiced fertility-centered polytheism: El, Baal, Asherah, Dagon, Molech, and Astarte, worshiped at high places. Israel was called to worship the one LORD (Yahweh) alone, though it often drifted into Baal worship. In Jesus’ day, Judaism was practiced under Roman rule, alongside Samaritans and pagan Greeks and Romans.
leaders: Patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob
Moses and Joshua
Judges: Deborah, Gideon, Samson, Samuel
United kingdom: Saul, David, Solomon (c. 1050–930 BC)
Divided kingdom: Jeroboam, Ahab, Hezekiah, Josiah and others
Governors and kings under Rome: Herod the Great, Pontius Pilate
story: The Promised Land. Abraham was told to walk through it, Joshua led Israel into it, David made Jerusalem its capital, and Solomon built the Temple. It split into Israel (north) and Judah (south) around 930 BC. The whole story of Jesus and the early church begins here.

name: Phoenicia
modern: Lebanon, with coastal Syria and northern Israel
religion: Polytheistic. Phoenicians worshiped Baal (Melqart at Tyre), Astarte, Eshmun, and El. Cities practiced temple worship and sometimes child sacrifice.
leaders: Hiram I of Tyre, who supplied cedar and craftsmen for David and Solomon (1 Kings 5)
Ethbaal of Sidon, father of Jezebel (1 Kings 16:31)
Jezebel, the Phoenician princess who married Ahab
story: A seafaring trading nation of city-states (Tyre, Sidon, Byblos) and the source of the cedars of Lebanon for the Temple. The prophets condemned Tyre’s pride (Ezekiel 26–28). Jesus visited the region of Tyre and Sidon (Mark 7).

name: Aram (Syria)
modern: Syria (Damascus, Aleppo) and parts of southern Turkey
religion: Polytheistic. Arameans worshiped Hadad (Rimmon), the storm god, along with Atargatis and local gods. Damascus had a temple of Rimmon (2 Kings 5:18).
leaders: Ben-Hadad I and II of Damascus (1 Kings 15, 20)
Naaman, commander healed by Elisha (2 Kings 5)
Hazael, who oppressed Israel (2 Kings 8–13)
Rezin, who joined Israel against Judah (Isaiah 7)
Aretas IV, ruling Damascus when Paul escaped (2 Corinthians 11:32)
story: A frequent rival of northern Israel. Aramaic later became the common language of the Near East, and Jesus likely spoke it. Paul met Jesus on the road to Damascus (Acts 9), and Antioch became the base of early Gentile mission.

name: Edom, Moab & Ammon
religion: Polytheistic. Chemosh was the god of Moab, Milcom (Molech) of Ammon, and Qos of Edom. Their peoples descended from Lot (Moab, Ammon) and Esau (Edom), relatives of Israel.
leaders: Balak of Moab, who hired Balaam (Numbers 22)
Mesha of Moab, who rebelled against Israel (2 Kings 3)
Nahash of Ammon (1 Samuel 11)
Hadad the Edomite (1 Kings 11)
Herod the Great, from Idumea (Edom)
story: Kingdoms east and south of the Dead Sea, often at war with Israel. Ruth was a Moabite who became an ancestor of David. In the New Testament era Nabataean Arabs ruled from Petra.

name: Arabia & Midian
modern: Saudi Arabia, with parts of Yemen, Oman, and the Gulf states
religion: Polytheistic. Desert peoples worshiped star, moon and sun gods and local deities at sacred stones. Midianite Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, was a priest who honored the LORD (Exodus 18).
leaders: Jethro, priest of Midian (Exodus 3, 18)
The Queen of Sheba (Sheba was in southern Arabia; 1 Kings 10)
Ishmael’s twelve sons as tribal chiefs (Genesis 25)
Oreb and Zeeb, Midianite princes (Judges 7)
story: Moses fled here and met God at the burning bush. Caravans carrying incense and gold traveled from southern Arabia to Israel, and Paul spent time in Arabia after his conversion (Galatians 1:17).

name: Assyria
modern: Northern Iraq (Mosul/Nineveh), with parts of southeastern Turkey and northeastern Syria
religion: Polytheistic. Ashur was the national god, with Ishtar, Sin, Shamash, and Nabu also worshiped. The king was chief priest of Ashur, and campaigns were held to be holy war.
leaders: Shalmaneser III (858–824 BC)
Tiglath-Pileser III / Pul (2 Kings 15–16)
Shalmaneser V and Sargon II, who ended the northern kingdom in 722 BC (2 Kings 17)
Sennacherib, who besieged Jerusalem in 701 BC (2 Kings 18–19)
Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal
story: The brutal superpower that destroyed northern Israel. Jonah was sent to preach to Nineveh, and its people repented. Nahum later foretold Nineveh’s fall (612 BC).

name: Babylonia
modern: Central and southern Iraq (Babylon lies near Hillah, south of Baghdad)
religion: Polytheistic. Marduk was the chief god of Babylon, with Nabu, Ishtar, and Sin. Babylonians practiced astrology and divination, and built ziggurats such as the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11).
leaders: Nimrod, the great hunter (Genesis 10)
Hammurabi (c. 1792–1750 BC)
Nebuchadnezzar II, who destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC (2 Kings 25)
Evil-Merodach, who freed Jehoiachin (2 Kings 25:27)
Belshazzar (Daniel 5)
story: Home to Ur, where Abram was born, and later the empire that carried Judah into exile. Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego served here, and Ezekiel and Jeremiah wrote to the exiles.

name: Persia (Media & Elam)
modern: Iran (with the empire also covering Iraq, Turkey, and Egypt at its peak)
religion: Zoroastrianism was the royal religion, with Ahura Mazda as the supreme god and a dualist struggle between good and evil. Persian kings were generally tolerant, and Cyrus credited the LORD with giving him his kingdoms (Ezra 1:2).
leaders: Cyrus the Great, who freed the Jews in 538 BC (Ezra 1; Isaiah 45)
Darius I (Ezra 6; Haggai)
Xerxes I / Ahasuerus (Esther)
Artaxerxes I, who sent Ezra and Nehemiah (Ezra 7; Nehemiah 2)
story: Persia conquered Babylon in 539 BC and allowed exiles to return and rebuild the Temple. Esther became queen here, and the magi who visited Jesus came from the east (Matthew 2).

name: Asia Minor (Hittites & Lydia)
religion: Hittites worshiped the storm god Teshub and “a thousand gods.” Later, Greek and Roman cults (Artemis of Ephesus, Zeus, Cybele) filled the cities, alongside Jewish synagogues across the region.
leaders: Ephron the Hittite, who sold Abraham a burial cave (Genesis 23)
Uriah the Hittite, husband of Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11)
Croesus of Lydia
Roman governors of Asia, Galatia, and Cappadocia
story: Once home to the Hittite empire, and in the New Testament the setting for Paul’s journeys through Galatia, Ephesus, and Colossae, and for the seven churches of Revelation.

name: Greece & Macedonia
modern: Greece, North Macedonia, and southern Albania
religion: Polytheistic. Greeks worshiped Zeus, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, and the rest of the Olympian gods, and prized philosophy. Paul found an altar “to an unknown god” in Athens (Acts 17:23).
leaders: Alexander the Great (336–323 BC), who spread Greek culture across the Near East (Daniel 8; 1 Maccabees 1)
Antiochus IV Epiphanes, a Greek-Syrian ruler who desecrated the Temple
Gallio, Roman proconsul of Achaia (Acts 18:12)
story: Greek became the common language of the New Testament world. Paul founded churches at Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, and Corinth, and preached on the Areopagus in Athens.

name: Rome (Italy)
modern: Italy (the Roman Empire eventually ruled the whole Mediterranean, including Israel)
religion: Polytheistic, with the state cult honoring Jupiter, Mars, Vesta, and others. From Augustus on, emperors were worshiped, which put Christians who refused into conflict with the state. Mystery religions and Judaism also flourished.
leaders: Augustus, who ordered the census (Luke 2:1)
Tiberius, emperor during Jesus’ ministry (Luke 3:1)
Claudius, who expelled Jews from Rome (Acts 18:2)
Nero, who persecuted Christians
Pontius Pilate and Herod Antipas, as Roman-appointed rulers in Judea and Galilee
story: The superpower of the New Testament. Roman roads and peace made the rapid spread of the gospel possible. Paul appealed to Caesar and was taken to Rome, where Acts ends (Acts 28).
